talks.title: Device Code Phishing Is Dead, Long Live New Azure AD Attacks!
talks.teaser: Elias Issa examines Device Code Phishing Is Dead, Long Live New Azure AD Attacks!.
talks.summary:
Overview: Elias, head of red team at Orange Cyberdefense, presents at Insomni'hack on new Azure AD attack vectors beyond device code phishing, including techniques validated in four red team operations.

Key Topics: Azure AD authentication mechanisms and their attack surfaces; device code phishing limitations; new social engineering vectors for token theft; password spraying effectiveness; and coordination with Microsoft on disclosure.

Technical Details: Elias demonstrates attack flows where victims receive codes to enter on legitimate Microsoft sites, completing authentication including MFA. He also covers password spraying against valid email lists with common passwords, noting its continued effectiveness despite visibility.

Takeaways: Azure AD's diverse authentication options create multiple attack paths beyond device code phishing. Organizations should monitor for anomalous authentication patterns and enforce strong password policies.

talks.title: Unmasking A Novel Google Drive Phishing Chain
talks.teaser: Bobby Rauch analyzes Unmasking A Novel Google Drive Phishing Chain.
talks.summary:
Personal Discovery of the Campaign

The speaker, an Amazon offensive security engineer presenting personally, recounts receiving a Google Drive iOS push notification warning his storage was nearly full—a believable premise because his Drive actually was full. The notification originated from a random Micah Dean account on driaz.onmicrosoft.com, not Google.

Attacker Infrastructure Patterns

Threat actors easily spin up Microsoft 365 tenants with multiple onmicrosoft.com domains, rotating burned infrastructure. Guardz tracking shows large numbers of randomly generated tenants used for phishing. The HTML storage alert leads victims through a multi-step chain rather than a simple email link.

Evasion and Payload Delivery

To evade email security, attackers host lures on S3 objects with redirectors pointing to pages such as cloudstoragecentral.com hosted in Moldova, correlating with UNC5537 activity. Victims clicking secure storage are pushed toward Total Drive installers whose pre- and post-install scripts can hide malicious payloads, illustrating how trusted cloud brands cloak affiliate scam delivery.

talks.title: Cybersecurity Between Geopolitics And Tech Supremacy
talks.teaser: Florian Schütz investigates Cybersecurity Between Geopolitics And Tech Supremacy.
talks.summary:
Flawed Attack-Defense Framing

A Swiss federal defense speaker argues pure “we are attacked, we must defend” thinking puts defenders on a losing budget curve. Effective strategy also raises attacker costs—most incidents are criminal enterprises sensitive to ROI—and accepts breaches while shaping cheaper, resilient environments.

From Dot-Com Optimism to Geopolitics

Cyberspace was once framed economically after the dot-com boom, echoing John Perry Barlow’s Davos declaration that technology democratizes and frees cyberspace from government. Snowden-era revelations and great-power competition shifted technology policy toward security, intelligence, and control of networks.

Semiconductor and AI Supremacy

Modern flashpoints include AI productivity, 5G reach, and fab concentration—only TSMC and Samsung make leading chips; ASML dominates lithography tools. Geopolitical imperatives now push regionalized supply chains, US/EU fab investments, AI weapons/surveillance uses, and attempts to deny rivals access to advanced stacks.

Europe’s Strategic Choices

Europe lacks a full independent tech stack versus US and Chinese ecosystems; building one would take decades. The speaker notes European strengths in analog chips for guided weapons, urges realistic AI power constraints, and warns digital sovereignty rhetoric often ignores economic and energy limits.

talks.title: Livestreaming From North Korea's IT Workers Laptop Farm
talks.teaser: Mauro Eldritch analyzes Livestreaming From North Korea's IT Workers Laptop Farm.
talks.summary:
North Korean IT worker threat

Mauro and Einar Garcia Perez at Insomnihack detail Famous Chollima, a Lazarus-linked unit conducting remote IT worker fraud, corporate espionage, and revenue generation for the DPRK regime across finance, healthcare, engineering, and expanding sectors including real estate and pharma.

Honeypot operation

In a first-of-its-kind sting with Finers, BCIT, and ANY.RUN, they built a fake laptop farm/sandbox mimicking contractor environments, monitored GitHub recruitment spam, infiltrated handler networks, and recorded operatives from initial login through job-scam attempts.

GitHub tradecraft

Stage one tracked GitHub spammers using repetitive outreach templates, cloned profile images, rapid follower inflation, and clustering of related accounts. Stage two containment observed full attacker behavior inside isolated ANY.RUN laptop sandboxes, yielding technical indicators for defenders hiring remote developers.

talks.title: SACL: The Detection Capability You've Been Ignoring
talks.teaser: Wojtek Sochacki examines SACL: The Detection Capability You've Been Ignoring.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Marouane Aloui and Wojtek argue SOC teams overlook Windows System Access Control Lists (SACLs)—built-in auditing that closes EDR visibility gaps.

## EDR Blind Spots
Endpoint tools excel at writes and deletes but often miss file reads, subtle Active Directory object access, and policy differences across agent versions—gaps discovered painfully mid-incident.

## SACL Mechanics
Unlike DACLs (who may access an object), SACLs log allowed and denied attempts to the Security event log—like cameras recording every door try. They apply to files, registry keys, and AD objects without extra agents.

## Takeaways
Detection engineering should instrument high-value assets with SACLs for read/access auditing, complementing EDR rather than waiting on vendor roadmaps.

talks.title: Pentesting By The Numbers: What Data Analysis Tells About What We Do by Charl Van Der Walt
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Pentesting By The Numbers: What Data Analysis Tells About What We Do by Charl Van Der Walt.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Charl van der Walt (Head of Security Research at Orange Cyber Defense) explores whether vulnerability scanners and penetration testers are actually helping organizations defend against real-world threats. Using an extensive dataset spanning millions of vulnerability scanning findings and roughly 1,500 penetration testing reports, van der Walt investigates the disconnect between vulnerabilities actively exploited by threat actors and those discovered and reported by security professionals.

### Key Topics
- **Vulnerability Management Overload:** With ~18,000 new CVEs annually and an average of 18–19 actionable findings per host, organizations struggle to patch more than 5% to 20% of known flaws, even though only an estimated 2% to 7% are ever exploited in the wild.
- **Data Ingestion & Methodology:** Vulnerability scan data from scanners like Qualys and Rapid7 was aggregated via Nucleus across 41,000 hosts (~3 million findings). Penetration test reports (Word documents) were unzipped, parsed via XML, anonymized, and processed using spaCy NLP for Named Entity Recognition (NER) to extract CVEs and metadata across ~1,500 assessments.
- **Remediation Timelines & Demographics:** Across scanning data, remediating a vulnerability takes an average of 215 days (72% take >30 days, 52% take >90 days). Critical vulnerabilities are resolved ~35% faster, yet still average over six months. Furthermore, 47% of reported CVEs across scanning and pen testing were over five years old.
- **Comparative Exploit Datasets:** The speaker compared customer vulnerability exposure and pen tester findings against three threat intelligence benchmarks:
  1. *Ivanti Ransomware Top 10:* Only 5 of the top 10 appeared in customer scans, and only 1 (Log4j) was ever exploited by pen testers across 1,500 assessments (exploited exactly once).
  2. *CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV):* 52% of the ~860 KEV vulnerabilities never appeared across 41,000 customer hosts. Of the remaining KEV vulnerabilities present, pen testers reported only 7 unique CVEs.
  3. *FIRST Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS v3):* EPSS demonstrates that targeting a low threshold (0.088) achieves 82% exploit coverage by patching only 7.3% of vulnerabilities (45% efficiency), compared to CVSS >= 7 requiring 58% of all CVEs to be patched (3.9% efficiency). Evaluating vulnerabilities with an EPSS score > 0.03 present in customer environments, pen testers reported zero of them.
- **Trends Over Time:** Between 2018 and 2022, penetration tests exhibited a downward trend in findings per day (measured in CVSS per day) and a drop in serious findings from 71% in Q4 2018 down to 33% in Q1 2022. Potential causes discussed include improved base security from modern cloud frameworks, recurring customer maturation, and remote testing constraints over VPN post-2020.
- **Complex Attack Realities:** Referencing the LastPass breach, van der Walt highlighted how real-world intrusions often link disjointed components (credential compromise, shared cloud backups, developer home networks, and targeted software flaws like Plex CVE-2020-5741) that isolated scanning and testing rarely capture or prioritize.

### Technical Details
- **Metrics:** Introduced "CVSS per day" (total CVSS points divided by man-days) to normalize pen testing output. Internal tests yielded the highest volume (~8 CVSS points/day), while red teaming yielded the lowest (~2 CVSS points/day) due to fewer, higher-severity findings.
- **Scoring & Distributions:** Vulnerability scanners and pen testers both heavily report medium-severity issues (peaking around CVSS 4–5). Pen testers moderate ratings with context, rarely assigning maximum severity scores and occasionally assigning 0, whereas scanners assign higher critical volumes.

### Takeaways
Security assessments often suffer from an emulation disconnect, echoing Haroon Meer's critique that pen testers often emulate other pen testers rather than real threat actors. While organizations invest heavily in web application gymnastics and chasing CVSS scores, real attackers repeatedly rely on credential stuffing, phishing, password reuse, and specific unpatched perimeter services. Security programs must re-evaluate prioritize-by-CVSS models and leverage data-driven intelligence like EPSS to focus on the small fraction of vulnerabilities that attackers actually exploit.

talks.title: Adversary Tracking And All The Lies We Tell Ourselves by Joe Slowik
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Adversary Tracking And All The Lies We Tell Ourselves by Joe Slowik.
talks.aiSummary:
## Overview

In the presentation *"Adversary Tracking And All The Lies We Tell Ourselves,"* Joe Slowik—head of threat detection/intelligence development, detection engineering, and threat hunting at Huntress, as well as founder of Perales—examines how the cybersecurity industry defines and conceptualizes threat actors. Slowik argues that traditional mental models and industry tropes surrounding adversaries are often overly simplistic and fail to reflect the operational realities of modern offensive campaigns.

## Defining the "Adversary"

Slowik contrasts common cultural tropes—such as the stereotypical hoodie-wearing hacker, official state-sponsored wanted posters, or flamboyant e-crime figures posing with Lamborghinis—with standard industry definitions. Referencing the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), an adversary is formally defined as:

* A person, group, organization, or government that conducts or has the intent to conduct detrimental activities against an entity.

While many in the security community use the word "attack," Slowik highlights that NIST's phrasing of "detrimental activities" is intentional, noting that "attack" can be unnecessarily narrow or strong for certain cyber activities.

## The Myth of the Monolithic Threat Actor

A primary flaw in contemporary threat intelligence is the assumption that adversaries (such as Lazarus Group, Conti, Equation Group, or APT28) operate as unified, monolithic single entities handling every phase of an operation. 

Slowik explains that modern offensive operations—whether state-sponsored, criminal, or even red team/penetration testing—are fundamentally complex and specialized:

* **Specialization and Division of Labor:** Single individuals or groups rarely manage every stage of the cyber kill chain or fill out every category in the MITRE ATT&CK matrix alone. Doing everything in-house is inefficient and impractical.
* **Cooperation and Ecosystems:** Operators rely on teams with specialized skill sets. Different entities specialize in developing malware, managing infrastructure, or executing initial access, and then interoperate, collaborate, or broker/sell access to other actors.
* **Separation of Roles:** In state-centric and organized cyber environments, operations are structured with distinct layers: an overriding authority or customer providing strategic direction and mission objectives, distinct groups responsible for developing technical capabilities and writing malware, and dedicated operators executing the intrusion.

## Key Takeaways for Security Disciplines

Treating sophisticated adversaries as single, monolithic actors creates blind spots for defenders. Understanding the distributed nature of modern cyber operations—disentangling capability developers, access brokers, and operators—is essential not only for threat intelligence analysts, but also for detection development, red teaming, and adversary emulation exercises.

talks.title: Permissionless Android Universal Overlays by Dimitrios Valsamaras
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Permissionless Android Universal Overlays by Dimitrios Valsamaras.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Dimitrios Valsamaras, Senior Security Researcher at Microsoft Threat Intelligence and former Google Play Store malware review lead, presents research on universal Android overlay attacks that require no permissions. The presentation analyzes Android's graphics architecture, window management lifecycle, and the historical evolution of UI confusion and tapjacking attacks. Valsamaras demonstrates how systemic design behaviors in window management and backward-compatibility mechanisms allow malicious applications to display deceptive overlays over victim apps without declaring or requesting the sensitive SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission.

Key Topics:
- Android graphics stack architecture (View, Surface, WindowManagerService, SurfaceFlinger, Hardware Composer)
- Window Z-ordering, window types, and permission requirements (SDK < 23 backward compatibility)
- Window event dispatching flags (FLAG_NOT_TOUCHABLE click-through behavior)
- Permissionless universal overlay creation and free-floating process-bound windows

Technical Details:
In Android, user interface components (Views) are backed by Surface objects managed by SurfaceFlinger, which coordinates with the Hardware Composer HAL for final on-screen display composition. The ordering, positioning, focus, and lifecycle animations of these surfaces are dictated by the WindowManagerService (WMS). Applications interact with WMS indirectly via WindowManager and WindowManager.LayoutParams. Windows reside along a vertical Z-order axis determined by window types. Historically, high-priority overlay windows (such as TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY or deprecated TYPE_SYSTEM_ALERT) sat atop the Z-axis to display floating elements across the OS, requiring the dangerous SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW permission.

The speaker reveals how Android maintains backward compatibility for legacy applications. Prior to Android SDK 23 (Android 6.0 Marshmallow), SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW was granted automatically at install time. When modern Android versions run applications targeting SDK versions lower than 23, the platform automatically approves the overlay permission by default. Furthermore, window behavioral flags alter how input events are processed. By applying FLAG_NOT_TOUCHABLE, an overlay window instructs the window manager to ignore user touches and transparently dispatch click events to whatever underlying window sits below, enabling stealthy click-through tapjacking without requiring special user-facing permissions.

Windows added through WindowManager.addView() exhibit process-level persistence rather than activity-level coupling. Once created, these free-floating windows remain active on screen even after the originating application's Activity is dismissed, as long as the parent background process remains alive. Threat actors and Android banking malware exploit this decoupling alongside unprivileged window types to create universal overlays without user notification. By synchronizing overlay instantiation with background task-switching telemetry, a permissionless malware app can project deceptive authentication prompts or disguise malicious consent dialogues over legitimate banking, corporate, or system applications.

Key Takeaways:
Android application developers must harden sensitive activities by setting filterTouchesWhenObscured to true to prevent obscured touch dispatching and tapjacking attacks. Operating system vendors must restrict backward compatibility affordances, strictly enforcing runtime permission checks even for apps targeting legacy SDKs below level 23. Mobile threat detection solutions must monitor process-bound floating windows and correlate WindowManager calls with background application states to detect unauthorized UI overlays.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Turn And Face The Strange: Ch-Ch-Changes In Ransomware Techniques by Lindsay Kaye
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Turn And Face The Strange: Ch-Ch-Changes In Ransomware Techniques by Lindsay Kaye.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Lindsay Kaye, Senior Director of Advanced Reversing Malware Operations and Reconnaissance at Recorded Future's Insikt Group, examines recent tactical, techniques, and procedures (TTP) changes across the ransomware ecosystem. Driven by market pressures and competition, ransomware groups actively innovate their tooling, delivery, and extortion strategies. However, these technical shifts do not always produce their intended effects; poorly planned or executed features frequently backfire, introducing exploitable flaws, distinct signature artifacts, and opportunities for defensive hunting.

### Key Topics
- **Evolution of Delivery and Extortion**: Attackers increasingly utilize benign tools, MSP software, SMB/CIFS/NFS shares, and impersonation tokens for lateral movement. To force ransom payments, threat actors deploy multi-faceted extortion, including DDoS attacks, direct outreach to executives and journalists, and printing ransom notes directly via network printers.
- **Language Transitions and Architecture Targeting**: Groups have shifted from traditional C/C++ to languages like Rust, Go, and Python. Furthermore, operators are releasing specialized lockers for Linux, VMware ESXi, and ARM architectures (targeting NAS platforms like QNAP and Synology).
- **Speed via Intermittent Encryption**: Attackers such as Play, ALPHV, Black Basta, and Agenda encrypt data intermittently (e.g., alternating 1 MB blocks) to maximize encryption speed and evade detection while preventing easy file recovery.
- **Flawed Tooling and Obfuscation**: Custom obfuscation frameworks (such as ALPHV's Morph toolkit) and homemade cryptographic implementations frequently result in bloat, reverse-engineering aids (like unstripped symbol names), or catastrophic decryption bugs that allow victim file recovery without payment.
- **Code Reuse and Rebranding**: Leaked source code and builders (notably BlackMatter, Conti, and REvil) fuel multiple offshoots, including LockBit Black and LockBit Green, as well as false-flag attribution efforts.

### Technical Details
- **Play Ransomware**: Written in C++, Play introduced a minimal ransom note and intermittent encryption (encrypting every other 1 MB). In August 2022, Play incorporated Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) gadgets using `ret` instructions to jump to actual code, alongside automated garbage code insertion and API hashing. While ROP complicated static analysis, the automated garbage code proved highly signatureable.
- **ALPHV (BlackCat)**: Emerging as a rebrand of BlackMatter/DarkSide, ALPHV introduced a cross-platform Rust codebase, an ARM variant for NAS devices, and build-time chat access tokens requiring parameters to prevent security researchers from discovering active victim negotiation links. Its "Morph" obfuscation engine utilized a 1-byte XOR key and dead arithmetic code on Windows, expanding binary sizes over fourfold. On 64-bit Linux/ESXi builds, Morph failed to obfuscate strings and left demangled function names containing references like `Locker` and core routines.
- **Cryptographic Blunders**: ESXiArgs' early variant calculated skip offsets based on file size, skipping approximately 4.5 GB in large virtual machine disks (leaving data largely intact). Luna failed to stop VMs before encrypting them, causing data corruption. DarkSide and BlackMatter rolled custom crypto with flaws that enabled researchers to create free decrypters.
- **LockBit Evolution & Code Lineage**: LockBit deployed the "StealBit" automated exfiltration utility and actively solicited enterprise insiders for initial access. Following leaks of BlackMatter and Conti source code, LockBit created LockBit Black and LockBit Green. LockBit Black retained BlackMatter's architecture, anti-debugging tricks (such as crashing when a breakpoint is placed on a thread), and configuration formats, while adding password-based execution/decryption flags and extended command-line options.
- **False-Flag Attribution**: Threat actors frequently attempt misdirection, such as LockBit claiming Chinese residency, or groups posting machine-translated Chinese on forums like RAMP. In one case, a group claiming to be Chinese (Yanluowang) had internal Russian chat logs leaked, while samples of "Xiao" ransomware reused REvil's "Revix 1.1" Linux locker codebase.

### Takeaways
Defenders and malware analysts can capitalize on threat actor mistakes to hunt and disrupt ransomware operations. Tracking automated obfuscation artifacts, compiler-specific runtime anomalies, odd string misspellings, anti-analysis patterns, and code reuse across leaked builders provides powerful pivot points for detecting emerging ransomware variants.

talks.title: (KEYNOTE) The Converging Threat Landscape by Patrice Perche
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning (KEYNOTE) The Converging Threat Landscape by Patrice Perche.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this keynote address, Patrice Perche discusses the escalating challenges across the cybersecurity threat landscape and Fortinet’s perspectives on counteracting global cybercrime. Organizations are grappling with rapid infrastructure changes—such as hybrid work models, application decentralization across edges and clouds, IT/OT convergence, and tool sprawl. Concurrently, cybercriminals are scaling operations through advanced tooling and convergence with nation-state methods. The presentation outlines telemetry observed through FortiGuard Labs, regional threat trends in Switzerland, predictive indicators around destructive malware and Crime-as-a-Service, and the critical need for cross-sector collaboration between public and private entities.

### Key Topics
- **Infrastructure Evolution & Complexity:** The shift toward hybrid work and cloud adoption increases management friction. Securing operational technology (OT) and critical infrastructure is increasingly vital as legacy systems converge with standard IT networks. Fortinet advocates for vendor and tool consolidation, secure networking (e.g., Secure SD-WAN/Secure Branch), and mesh architectures.
- **Threat Intelligence & Telemetry:** Insights into FortiGuard Labs' data ingestion, which uses roughly 10 million deployed network appliances as sensors, monitors 200 billion daily threat events, and leverages machine learning to scale threat evaluation and augment security operations.
- **Regional Insights (Switzerland):** Data from 2022 ranks Switzerland fourth in overall attacks within the EMEA region (accounting for ~9% of worldwide attacks recorded by Fortinet). Notable attack waves included Log4j in Q1 2022 and IoT/OT Mirai botnet activity targeting manufacturing in Q4 2022.
- **Evolution of Cybercrime & APT Convergence:** Traditional cybercrime syndicates and advanced persistent threat (APT) groups are increasingly merging tactics, infrastructure, and target sets into what Perche terms "Advanced Persistent Cybercrime."
- **Public-Private Collaboration:** Actionable disruption requires shared intelligence and unified action through initiatives such as the World Economic Forum's Cybercrime Atlas, the Cyber Threat Alliance, MITRE R&D, and law enforcement operations with Interpol.

### Technical Details
- **Zero-Day Vulnerability Research:** Fortinet operates a responsible disclosure program, working directly with vendors (including over 80 partners like Microsoft, Siemens, Schneider Electric, ABB, and GE) to patch flaws and implement virtual patches via IPS engines before wide exploitation.
- **Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) Shifts:** Criminal operations have shifted from high-volume, broad affiliate networks (~1,000 partners) to more selective models (~100 partners), concentrating heavily on Very Large Enterprises (VLE) and OT/manufacturing. This targeted approach has seen ransom demands transition from seven-figure to eight-figure sums.
- **Surge in Wiper Malware:** Destructive wiper malware grew substantially throughout 2022. FortiGuard Labs tracked 16 new wiper variants in 2022 compared to historical norms of roughly one per year. While early 2022 activity was concentrated on Ukraine, wipers expanded globally into cross-platform targets (Windows, Linux, Unix, Solaris), averaging 13,000 monthly attacks in Q4 2022 (a 53% quarter-over-quarter increase).
- **Expansion of Crime-as-a-Service (CaaS):** Commodity services on the dark web now span DDoS-as-a-Service, phishing, stolen credentials, and reconnaissance, with threat actors weaponizing generative AI tools (such as ChatGPT/GPT-4) for reconnaissance and deepfake creation.
- **Law Enforcement Cooperation:** Practical outcomes highlighted include working with Interpol to dismantle a $16 million business email compromise (BEC) operation in Nigeria and ongoing operations targeting ransomware syndicates.

### Takeaways
Defending against contemporary cyber threats requires moving past isolated perimeter defenses toward an integrated security fabric and zero trust architectures that verify identity and behavior continuously. Because cybercriminals operate across jurisdictions with disparate legal frameworks, private organizations cannot succeed in isolation. Effective defense hinges on proactive cross-industry intelligence sharing, vendor consolidation to eliminate security gaps, and institutional partnerships linking technology vendors, enterprises, and international law enforcement.

talks.title: Breaking Docker's Named Pipes SYSTEMatically by Eviatar Gerzi
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Breaking Docker's Named Pipes SYSTEMatically by Eviatar Gerzi.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk presented at Insomniac, security researcher Eviatar Gerzi shares findings from an assessment into Docker Desktop on Windows and Windows containers. While Docker Desktop relies on several processes to run containers, it introduces an architectural attack surface between low-privileged user-facing components (such as the GUI) and privileged backend services like `com.docker.service`, which runs as `SYSTEM`. Communication across this boundary is handled via Windows named pipes, exposing undocumented REST-like endpoints that can be systematically abused by local users.

### Key Topics
- **Docker for Windows Architecture**: Breakdown of components including the Docker Desktop GUI, `dockerd`, and the Windows-specific privileged `com.docker.service` communicating via approximately 40 named pipes.
- **Implicit Privileged Group (`docker-users`)**: Analysis of the `docker-users` group, which Docker treats as unprivileged, but functionally grants administrative and `SYSTEM` compromise capabilities.
- **Named Pipe REST API Exposure**: Discovery of an undocumented HTTP client / REST API exposed over named pipes (`dockerBackendV2`) by `com.docker.service`.
- **Privilege Escalation Primitives**: Leveraging exposed APIs (`moveDataFolder`, `daemon.json` configuration, `pidfile`, and Hyper-V controller methods) to achieve arbitrary file writes, moves, and deletions, which are escalated to `SYSTEM` code execution using junction and symlink techniques.

### Technical Details
Gerzi identified that Windows containers inherently allow local privilege escalation to `SYSTEM` by design: a low-privileged user in `docker-users` can mount a protected host directory (such as `C:\Windows`) inside a container and modify host files directly from within the container. When reported, Docker stated this behavior was outside their control and suggested the `--no-windows-containers` flag.

Beyond this by-design limitation, the researcher analyzed the named pipe `dockerBackendV2` created by `ResolvePipeAsync` in `com.docker.service` dependency DLLs (`Docker.Core` and `Docker.Backend`), exposing REST API endpoints reachable by `docker-users`:
- **`moveDataFolder` Abuse**: Intended to move Docker VHDX data directories with `SYSTEM` privileges. While constrained by checks looking for `docker-desktop.vhdx`, subdirectories move all contents. Moving files across the same volume retains original low-privileged permissions. By combining directory junctions, James Forshaw's Object Manager symbolic links, and print spooler DLL hijacking (triggered without reboot via network service privilege escalation techniques documented by Alex Ionescu and Yarden Shafir), Gerzi gained an interactive `SYSTEM` shell on Windows 11.
- **`daemon.json` Start/Stop Configuration Manipulation**:
  - **`data-root`**: Setting the Docker data directory allows redirecting where configuration databases like `local-kv.db` are created. Exploiters can win a TOCTOU race condition by substituting a junction and symlink before file creation, yielding arbitrary file overwrite.
  - **`pidfile`**: Docker writes its process ID to a specified path on service start and deletes it on service stop using `DeleteFileW`. By targeting empty directory deletion (via `::$INDEX_ALLOCATION`) alongside Zero Day Initiative research (targeting `C:\Config.Msi` and malicious rollback scripts/HID DLL hijacking via on-screen keyboard `osk.exe`), arbitrary file deletion was turned into local privilege escalation.
- **Hyper-V Controller**: Methods `Create` and `Destroy` in the Hyper-V controller were similarly vulnerable to junction/symlink redirection, providing arbitrary file creation/overwrite and deletion primitives.

To aid research, Gerzi developed and referenced an inspection utility called `PipeViewer` to enumerate and audit named pipe permissions across Windows.

### Takeaways
Exposing rich, privileged REST-like APIs over Windows named pipes dramatically widens the local attack surface. Granting non-administrator accounts membership in the `docker-users` group effectively provides local administrative and `SYSTEM` equivalence on Windows hosts through built-in container volume mounting as well as flaws in Docker Desktop's backend services.

talks.title: Raising Employee Awareness: Which Training Strategy To Go For? by Eric Bärenzung
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Raising Employee Awareness: Which Training Strategy To Go For? by Eric Bärenzung.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Eric Bärenzung addresses the strategy and methodologies behind raising employee cybersecurity awareness. While human beings are often described as the "weakest link" in enterprise security, Bärenzung rejects this characterization. Instead, he highlights findings such as the Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report—which attributes 85% of breaches to human error—to argue that people are simply easy, frequent targets for cybercriminals. Consequently, the primary goal of security training must be to transform employees into an organization’s best allies and strongest security controls. Effective training requires explaining the fundamental "why," adapting content to institutional and regional culture, leveraging gamification, and establishing continuous, positive measurement rather than punitive practices.

### Key Topics
- **Establishing the "Why" and Executive Support**: Effective training starts by conveying why the company is at risk and why each person's role matters biologically and motivationally. Bärenzung stresses that security teams must approach company leadership not just with complaints, but with concrete solutions and specific asks to gain proper executive backing.
- **Content Formats and Cultural Fit**: Awareness programs should adopt varied delivery mechanisms—such as newsletters, booklets, lunch-and-learn sessions (e.g., at IWC), awareness months (European Cyber Security Month in October, Singapore in May), and branded physical items (mugs, mouse pads). When designing presentations, he references the 10/20/30 rule (10 slides, 20 minutes, large font) and optimal video lengths of 3 to 6 minutes. Furthermore, messaging and humor must respect distinct cultural contexts (e.g., France vs. Japan) and varying corporate environments (e.g., private banking vs. medtech startups).
- **Gamification and Modern Formats**: Incorporating friendly competition, escape rooms (e.g., ITV in the UK), and machine-learning-driven adaptive scenarios (such as an initiative at ZKB in Switzerland or kits by ANSSI in France) fosters voluntary participation and long-term engagement.
- **Measurement and Metrics**: Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) justify budgets and evaluate maturity (such as the SANS maturity model). Metrics should focus on positive outcomes—such as the frequency of incident reporting, quiz completion, user satisfaction, and questions raised to the security team—rather than solely phishing click rates, which can be noisy and discouraging. Bärenzung advocates running regular simulations (e.g., around eight phishing campaigns per year) without overloading users.

### Technical Details
Core training curriculums should balance classic hygiene topics with specialized engineering domains:
- **Primary Hygiene**: Phishing identification (accounting for an estimated 80% of threats in financial industries), password hygiene, avoiding malicious removable media/USB drives (noting cases of malware-laden USB drives mailed via postal services and historic incidents involving uranium facilities), mobile application security, and system patching.
- **Data Leak Prevention (DLP)**: Educating users on data classification schemes, proper file encryption, and steering staff away from unsecured internal emailing toward approved secure repositories (e.g., restricted SharePoint).
- **Advanced Subjects**: Specialized training where appropriate, including secure software development, IoT/embedded systems, quantum security, and crisis management exercises (referencing ITU exercises, such as one held in Moldova).

### Takeaways
- **No One-Size-Fits-All Approach**: Security awareness must be tailored to organization size, industry sector, regional culture, and individual employee expertise levels.
- **Avoid a Blame Culture**: Shaming or penalizing employees who fail phishing simulations discourages incident reporting and damages trust. Organizations should instead reward vigilance and positive reporting, comparing it to lottery-based positive reinforcement mechanisms rather than punitive ticketing.
- **Security Teams as Problem Solvers**: Rather than acting strictly as rigid enforcers who block tools or blacklist applications, security practitioners must explain risks clearly using real-world breach examples, offer direct alternatives, and engage through concise, personal meetings rather than repetitive broadcast emails.

talks.title: REW-sploit: Dissect Payloads With Ease by Cesare Pizzi
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning REW-sploit: Dissect Payloads With Ease by Cesare Pizzi.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Cesare Pizzi presents REW-sploit, an open-source reverse-engineering tool designed to analyze and extract artifacts from malicious payloads, particularly those generated by Metasploit and Cobalt Strike. Built on Unicorn Engine (a CPU emulator) and Mandiant Speakeasy, the tool addresses a gap in red-team tooling by providing defenders and reverse engineers with dynamic emulation-based analysis of encrypted and obfuscated payloads.

## Key Capabilities
REW-sploit automatically detects payload formats (32/64-bit shellcode, DLLs, executables) and performs emulation to extract API calls, encryption keys, configuration data, and other artifacts. For Metasploit payloads, it can extract RC4 and ChaCha encryption keys, identify C2 addresses, and decrypt second-stage payloads captured in PCAP files. For Meterpreter shells, it detects RSA/AES encryption handshakes and can force fallback to weaker encryption if the attacker's RSA public key import fails. Cobalt Strike beacon analysis extracts configuration, C2 parameters, and sleep masks even when heavily customized by attackers.

## Technical Approach
The tool uses dynamic emulation rather than static analysis to defeat obfuscation and encryption common in modern malware. Pizzi implemented numerous "fix-ups" to address emulation fragility—including workarounds for Shikata Ga Nai encoded code, floating-point instruction inconsistencies, stack size limitations, and API call failures in Unicorn/Speakeasy. The CLI-based interface supports features like memory allocation dumping, thread extraction, and anti-debug trick detection across 20+ known techniques.

## Supported Threats
Beyond Metasploit and Cobalt Strike, REW-sploit extends support to Donut (position-independent code conversion), PEzzer (packer), and SGN. Each integration required custom fix-ups to ensure reliable emulation. The tool is designed modular and extensible via YARA rules and Python scripting, allowing users to guide execution through specific code branches for deeper analysis.

## Advantages and Limitations
Advantages include defeating encryption and obfuscation without decryption keys, interactively modifying code execution to explore alternate branches, and rapid extraction of artifacts. Disadvantages include emulation fragility (not a true sandbox), slower execution, and a learning curve. Pizzi emphasizes this is not a replacement for traditional reverse-engineering tools like IDA or Ghidra but a complementary analysis accelerator.

## Project Status and Future Work
REW-sploit is at version 0.4 and open-source on GitHub. Pizzi actively contributes improvements back to upstream projects (Speakeasy, Unicorn) and seeks community contributions. Next steps include improved stability, performance optimization, expanded debug coverage, and broader platform support. The speaker encourages users to open issues and engage on GitHub for collaborative development.

talks.title: Hunting For Bugs In "Ethereum 2.0" by Denis Kolegov and JP Aumasson
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Hunting For Bugs In "Ethereum 2.0" by Denis Kolegov and JP Aumasson.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, JP Aumasson discusses security research on Ethereum consensus clients (formerly referred to as "Ethereum 2.0"), conducted under an Ethereum Foundation grant with collaborators Denis Kolegov and Evangelia Statopoulou. The talk covers the transition of Ethereum to Proof of Stake (PoS) via the Beacon Chain, the architecture of consensus clients, the audit methodology employed, and the vulnerability classes identified across cryptographic schemes, peer-to-peer transport, APIs, and dependencies.

### Key Topics
- **Beacon Chain & Client Ecosystem**: Overview of the Beacon Chain deployed in December 2020 to introduce Proof of Stake and data sharding. The talk reviews four primary consensus clients: Prysm (Go), Lighthouse (Rust), Teku (Java), and Nimbus (Nim). Each client functions as a server composed of a passive beacon node and an active validator node managing block proposals and attestations.
- **Audit Methodology**: The researchers compared implementation behavior across independent clients and checked code directly against official IETF drafts and Ethereum specifications to identify discrepancies in parameters, execution orders, and validation routines.
- **Cryptographic Schemes & P2P Protocols**: Analysis of BLS signatures, the libp2p networking stack, and the libp2p-noise (Noise_XX) secure transport handshake used between validators.
- **Software Supply Chain Risk**: Examination of third-party dependencies, transitive dependency graphs, and tooling (such as cargo-audit and dependabot) across different language ecosystems.

### Technical Details
- **BLS Signatures**: BLS signatures use hash-to-curve operations and scalar multiplication. The speaker highlighted edge cases such as handling point-at-infinity/zero inputs (which could allow forged signatures regardless of the secret key), missing subgroup checks, and detailed error messages acting as potential oracles. Across the four clients and specifications, the researchers identified 90 non-critical bug instances.
- **Noise Protocol Handshake & Transport**: In libp2p-noise, nodes exchange ephemeral keys and sign static keys with an identity key. The speaker noted vulnerabilities including potential replay attacks if key updates lack freshness tokens/challenges, and CPU DoS risks during initial handshake key exchanges. In the JavaScript/TypeScript implementation, an integer overflow bug originating from the Go noise-explorer code failed to stop after reaching 2^64 nonces, risking nonce reuse in AEAD ciphers. A separate TypeScript bug also resulted in unchecked signature verification.
- **APIs & Supply Chain**: HTTP REST and RPC/gRPC endpoints exhibited schema validation omissions, unauthenticated endpoints, and instances where API tokens were leaked into logs. In dependency analysis, Prysm had 665 total dependencies (93 direct) and Lighthouse had 440 total (121 direct), highlighting the difficulty of auditing deep dependency trees against malicious sabotage or backdoors.

### Takeaways
While no critical exploitable flaws allowing immediate theft of funds were discovered—largely due to extensive audits and fuzzing prior to the study—the complexity of distributed consensus mechanisms and asynchronous networks introduces subtle edge-case risks. Client diversity remains an important defense against network-wide outages, with Lighthouse singled out for strong security practices such as integrated CI fuzzing.

talks.title: From the cloud to the internal network - Offense vs Defense by Snir Ben-Shimol, Varonis
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in From the cloud to the internal network - Offense vs Defense by Snir Ben-Shimol, Varonis.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Snir Ben-Shimol, Director of Cybersecurity at Varonis, examines the evolving threat landscape as organizations migrate from on-premises Active Directory environments to hybrid and public cloud infrastructures (focusing heavily on Microsoft Azure and Office 365). Emphasizing the "assume breach" mindset, he explains that while perimeter controls inevitably fail, defense hinges on internal architecture, identity governance, and monitoring. He contrasts on-premise Active Directory concepts with Azure AD, breaks down attacker techniques across hybrid identities, and outlines detection and monitoring strategies for security operations center (SOC) and blue teams.

### Key Topics
- **Hybrid Cloud Identity Architecture:** Moving from on-prem Active Directory to Azure AD introduces fundamental differences in administration, permissions, service principals, subscriptions, and tenants. Trying to lift and shift on-prem policy mindsets into Azure AD creates substantial security gaps.
- **DevOps and Privileged Cloud Access:** DevOps users frequently receive broad subscription-level administrative privileges, functioning like modern domain administrators. Their credentials, access tokens, and access points are prime targets for initial compromise and privilege escalation.
- **Synchronization and Federation Risks:** Azure AD Connect utilizes highly privileged service accounts that replicate data and password hashes between on-prem and the cloud, presenting severe risks such as DCSync abuse. Similarly, Active Directory Federation Services (ADFS)DMZ servers host critical signing certificates; compromising these allows authentication into Azure AD.
- **MFA Limitations and Gaps:** Multi-Factor Authentication is an essential layer, but not a silver bullet. Highly privileged "break-glass" emergency access accounts are often explicitly configured without MFA per vendor recommendations. Additionally, legacy services, MSPs, and service accounts often lack MFA, while real-world adversary-in-the-middle phishing can intercept MFA tokens.
- **Reconnaissance via DNS:** Attackers favor DNS reconnaissance over Active Directory/LDAP queries to avoid triggering heavily monitored detection systems. Reverse lookups (PTR queries) allow mapping of network segmentation, servers, and hostnames while remaining disguised inside ordinary network traffic.
- **Cloud Data Sharing and Collaboration:** Features in SharePoint Online and Microsoft Teams permit direct or external file sharing that bypasses standard folder-level permissions, complicating access governance unless carefully audited and restricted.

### Technical Details
- **Azure AD Connect & DCSync:** Default or misconfigured permissions on Azure AD Connect synchronization service accounts can permit directory replication actions (DCSync), enabling attackers to harvest password hashes across the domain without being a full Domain Admin.
- **DNS Reconnaissance Detection:** Blue teams should monitor PTR queries (reverse DNS lookups) within internal subnets. Detection logic can filter out false positives by inspecting DNS authoritative flags and distinguishing internal queries from upstream queries sent outside the enterprise boundary, while accounting for multi-tier DNS forwarding.
- **Phishing & Credential Interception:** Attackers utilize Office 365/SharePoint Online brand impersonation, Punycode domain spoofing, and real-time phishing kits that request both passwords and live MFA tokens simultaneously to establish authenticated sessions.
- **Cloud Graph Auditing:** Blue teams can query the Azure AD Graph API to audit permission changes, monitor file-sharing events in SharePoint Online, and identify anomalous account delegations.
- **Insider Threat Case Study:** The speaker reviewed an incident where an 8-year IT administrator created an unprivileged shadow user account, granted it delegate access to executive mailboxes (CFO, Procurement, HR, team members), rapidly read dozens of emails across those accounts, accessed network shares containing salary spreadsheets, and exfiltrated zipped archives to a personal Gmail account.

### Takeaways
- **Assume Breach:** Security teams must focus on internal controls, least-privilege role assignment, and rapid anomaly detection rather than relying exclusively on boundary defenses or perimeter sandboxes.
- **Audit Non-MFA Accounts:** Organizations must systematically map and tightly monitor all accounts exempt from MFA, such as emergency access accounts, MSP accounts, and legacy service principals.
- **Lock Down Cloud Sharing:** Proactively disable global external file sharing in SharePoint Online/Teams where possible, enforce role-based access, and leverage file classification to alert on sensitive data exposure.
- **Behavioral Telemetry:** Correlating proxy upload logs, file activity, DNS query anomalies, and mailbox delegation changes provides early detection for both external adversaries and insider threats.

talks.title: Building a flexible hypervisor-level debugger by Mathieu Tarral (@mtarral)
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Building a flexible hypervisor-level debugger by Mathieu Tarral (@mtarral).
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation at Insomniac, Mathieu Tarral discusses how hypervisors can be leveraged as flexible, out-of-band debuggers using Virtual Machine Introspection (VMI). Traditional in-guest debuggers suffer from observer effects, anti-debugging mechanisms, privilege clashes with ring-0 malware, and interference with operating system protections like Windows PatchGuard and Protected Media Path. Debugging from the hypervisor allows security analysts to inspect untouched guest virtual machines transparently across platforms without modifying the target system or installing in-guest agents.

### Key Topics
- **Motivations and Concrete Use Cases**: Hypervisor-level debugging circumvents in-guest anti-debug techniques, enables kernel analysis without disabling security controls (such as PatchGuard), provides visibility into isolated environments (like Windows Virtual Secure Mode), and allows inspection of unikernels and early BIOS boot sequences (e.g., via BIOS interrupt `0x19`).
- **History and Ecosystem**: Prior efforts have spanned built-in debug stubs (e.g., QEMU, VMware), bare-metal hyperjacking/USB boot debuggers (HyperDBG, VerDBG, RomuFlex, VerOSDBG), emulation tools (Pyrebox), and full-virtualization introspection platforms (VMI DBG, RVM I, Winbagility/Sandboxity, and radare2-based approaches).
- **The Semantic Gap & Guest Awareness**: Hypervisors natively see only raw hardware state, registers, and memory addresses. Bridging the semantic gap requires intimate guest knowledge; tools like Rekall generate JSON profiles containing kernel structures, constants, and function offsets to translate raw offsets into meaningful processes, threads, and symbols.
- **PyVMI DBG Architecture**: Written in Python, PyVMI DBG serves as a GDB stub built on top of LibVMI to decouple front-end debuggers (GDB, radare2, IDA) from underlying hypervisors (such as Xen and KVM). It supports both raw mode (treating the whole VM as a single target where VCPUs map to threads) and guest-aware mode (inspecting specific processes like `cmd.exe`, enumerating threads, and handling break-ins).

### Technical Details
Tarral examines the design and evolution of "hyper breakpoints"—breakpoints executed via the virtualization layer:
- **Software Hyper Breakpoints (INT3)**: Overwriting guest memory with `0xCC` and trapping INT3 events. While fast, it is easily detected by memory scans and unsafe across multiple VCPUs unless all cores are paused to prevent race conditions during opcode restoration.
- **Hardware Hyper Breakpoints**: Using hardware debug registers (`DR0`–`DR3`) and handling INT1. These are per-VCPU safe and fast, with stealth achieved by intercepting `MOV to DR` instructions; however, they are restricted to four registers.
- **Page Hyper Breakpoints**: Modifying Extended Page Tables (EPT) to trigger EPT violations on read, write, or execute accesses. While fine-grained, this incurs heavy VM-exit overhead and suffers from multi-VCPU race conditions when permissions are relaxed.
- **Advanced Soft Hyper Breakpoints (EPT Shadow Views)**: Splitting memory views using processor EPT mechanisms (such as Xen's `altp2m` API, utilized by Drakvuf). A secondary EPT view points to a duplicated physical page containing the breakpoint set as execute-only, while the original page remains read-write. By switching the EPT pointer (`EPTP`) per VCPU upon EPT violations, the debugger achieves stealth, high performance, and multi-VCPU safety without triggering race conditions.

### Takeaways
Tarral advocates treating virtual machines not as black boxes, but as transparent process trees. To establish a unified debugging framework across hypervisors, Tarral calls for hypervisor vendors to expose standardized VMI APIs, encourages community contribution to LibVMI (including cross-platform CMake builds, performance optimizations via `/dev/shm`, driver support, and exploring rewrites in Rust for memory safety), and invites developers to expand PyVMI DBG with additional stubs (such as LLDB and KD).
